clips.text: Kartini was born on 21 April 1879 in Mayong, Jepara, into a Javanese noble family. She went to a Dutch school and loved to read.
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 1/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: At about 12 she had to leave school and stay at home, as custom required of noble girls then. Kartini badly wanted to keep learning.
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 2/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: From home she wrote letters to friends in the Netherlands. She wrote about the lives of Javanese women and her hope that girls could go to school.
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 3/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: In 1903 Kartini opened a small class for girls in her family's home in Jepara. After marrying the Regent of Rembang late that year, she taught in Rembang too.
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 4/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Kartini died in 1904, aged just 25. In 1911 her letters came out as a book, later known in Indonesian as "Habis Gelap Terbitlah Terang" (After Darkness Comes Light).
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 5/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Her birthday, 21 April, is celebrated as Kartini Day. Her story asks us to help every child, girl or boy, keep learning.
clips.note: Raden Ajeng Kartini (1879–1904): panel 6/6 of "Kartini and her letters" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Dewi Sartika was born on 4 December 1884 in Bandung, into a Sundanese noble family. Her parents sent her to a Dutch school, which was rare for girls then.
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 1/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: As a child she loved playing school. She taught the servants' children to read and write, using boards, charcoal and bits of roof tile.
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 2/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: At the time very few girls could go to school. Dewi Sartika wanted them to read, count and learn practical skills.
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 3/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: On 16 January 1904, with the support of the Regent of Bandung, she opened Sakola Istri (School for Girls) at the regency hall. Its first class had 20 girls.
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 4/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Pupils learned reading, writing and arithmetic, and also sewing, cooking and batik. In 1910 the school was renamed Sakola Kautamaan Istri (School of Women's Virtue).
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 5/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Dewi Sartika died in 1947 and was named a National Hero in 1966. Her story reminds us that shared knowledge can change many lives.
clips.note: Raden Dewi Sartika (1884–1947): panel 6/6 of "Dewi Sartika and the School for Girls" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Ki Hajar Dewantara was born in Yogyakarta on 2 May 1889 as Raden Mas Soewardi Soerjaningrat. He became a journalist who wrote boldly.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 1/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: In 1913 he wrote the article "If I Were a Dutchman". It criticised the colonial government's plan to collect money from residents, including Indonesians, to celebrate 100 years of Dutch independence.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 2/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Because of that article he was exiled to the Netherlands. There he used his time to study education and earned a teaching certificate.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 3/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: He came home in 1919, and on 3 July 1922 he founded Taman Siswa in Yogyakarta, a school for Indonesian children. He gave up his noble title and took the name Ki Hajar Dewantara.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 4/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: In 1932 a new colonial rule threatened private schools such as Taman Siswa. Ki Hajar opposed it without violence, and the rule was eventually withdrawn.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 5/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: He became Indonesia's first minister of education, and his birthday is now National Education Day. His motto, "Tut Wuri Handayani", means encouraging from behind.
clips.note: Ki Hajar Dewantara (1889–1959): panel 6/6 of "Ki Hajar Dewantara and Taman Siswa" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Mohammad Hatta was born in Bukittinggi, West Sumatra, on 12 August 1902. He later studied economics in the Netherlands for about ten years.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 1/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Because of his work in the national movement, he was exiled to Boven Digoel in Papua and later to Banda Neira. He took crates of books and kept reading and writing.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 2/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: On 17 August 1945, together with Sukarno, he proclaimed Indonesia's independence. He then became the Republic's first vice president.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 3/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Hatta believed ordinary people's livelihoods could grow strong through cooperatives, joint businesses built on mutual help. At the 1953 Cooperative Congress in Bandung he was named Father of Indonesian Cooperatives.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 4/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Hatta was known for honesty and a simple life: he always returned any unspent state money given for his duties. He once wanted a pair of shoes, but the money always went to other needs.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 5/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Hatta died in Jakarta on 14 March 1980. His example asks us to be honest in small things, even when no one is watching.
clips.note: Mohammad Hatta (1902–1980): panel 6/6 of "Hatta, books and honesty" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Zheng He, known in Indonesia as Cheng Ho, was born around 1371 in Yunnan, China, into a Muslim family. He became a trusted admiral of the Ming emperor.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 1/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: In 1405 the emperor sent him to lead a great voyage to lands across the sea. His first fleet had 62 large ships and about 27,800 people.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 2/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Between 1405 and 1433 his fleet made seven voyages. They called at Java, Sumatra and Malacca, then went on to India, the Persian Gulf and as far as East Africa.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 3/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Voyages that long depended on the compass, the stars and the monsoon winds. Sailors had to wait patiently for the right wind.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 4/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: His ships carried silk and porcelain and came home with goods and envoys from many lands. Zheng He died around 1433.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 5/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: In Semarang, the Sam Poo Kong site is linked to Cheng Ho's visit, and his name is remembered in many coastal towns. His story asks us to build ties with other nations peacefully and with respect.
clips.note: Zheng He / Cheng Ho (c. 1371–1433): panel 6/6 of "The voyages of Zheng He" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, on 24 February 1304. In 1325, aged 21, he set out on the hajj pilgrimage to Mecca.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 1/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: After the pilgrimage he did not head home. He chose to keep travelling and see more of the world.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 2/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: He travelled across North Africa, the Middle East and India. Around 1345 he stopped at Samudra Pasai in Sumatra, where the sultan gave him a ship to continue to China.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 3/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: His journeys were long and hard, across deserts and seas. All together his travels lasted almost 30 years.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 4/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: At the request of Morocco's sultan, he dictated his travels to the writer Ibn Juzayy. The book is known as the Rihla.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 5/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: He covered about 120,000 km, roughly three times around the Earth. His story asks us to get to know the world and respect people of every culture.
clips.note: Ibn Battuta (1304–1368/69): panel 6/6 of "The travels of Ibn Battuta" (Sejarah adults, sej-a).

clips.text: About 1,200 years ago Baghdad was a city of learning. Caliph al-Ma'mun supported the House of Wisdom, where scholars translated and wrote books.
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 1/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Al-Khwarizmi worked there as a mathematician and astronomer. He lived from about 780 to 850.
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 2/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: People needed orderly ways to work out inheritances, trade and measure land. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book for everyday problems like these.
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 3/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: In it he explained al-jabr, "completing", and al-muqabala, "balancing". The word al-jabr gave us the word "algebra".
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 4/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: He also wrote about the numerals from India, with place value and zero. A Latin translation carried them to Europe, and his name became the word "algorithm".
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 5/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Every time a phone works out a route or a price, it runs an algorithm. Al-Khwarizmi's story asks us to explain knowledge in clear steps.
clips.note: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–c. 850): panel 6/6 of "Al-Khwarizmi and algebra" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: In the 9th century Fez, in Morocco, was a busy, growing city. Many families from Kairouan, in today's Tunisia, settled there.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 1/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: According to the historian Ibn Abi Zar', writing in the 14th century, Fatima al-Fihri inherited the wealth of her merchant father. She decided to use it for the good of many people.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 2/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Around 859 she founded the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez. It became a place to gather, to pray and to learn.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 3/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Over time al-Qarawiyyin became a centre of learning that drew students from many lands. People studied religion, language and mathematics there.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 4/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Fatima's story was written down centuries after her death, so some historians doubt the details. But the institution linked to her still stands today.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 5/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Guinness World Records lists al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859, as the oldest higher-learning institution still running. Her story asks us to use what we have to open the way to learning for others.
clips.note: Fatima al-Fihri (c. 800–c. 880): panel 6/6 of "Fatima al-Fihri and al-Qarawiyyin" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born in 980 near Bukhara, in today's Uzbekistan. By the age of ten he had memorised the Qur'an.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 1/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: He began studying medicine at 13. By 16 he was already treating patients.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 2/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: After he cured the Samanid ruler, he was allowed to read in the royal library. There he learned from a great many books.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 3/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Unsettled times often forced him to move from city to city, but he kept writing. He died in Hamadan, Persia, in 1037.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 4/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: His great work, The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb), gathered the medical knowledge of his time. He wrote about 450 works, and about 240 survive.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 5/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: The Canon was translated into Latin in the 12th century and studied by medical students in Europe until the late 17th century. His story asks us to study hard and write knowledge down so it helps others.
clips.note: Ibn Sina / Avicenna (980–1037): panel 6/6 of "Ibn Sina and the Canon of Medicine" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Florence Nightingale was born on 12 May 1820 in Florence, Italy, to a wealthy English family. She wanted to be a nurse, work then seen as unsuitable for a woman of her class.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 1/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: In November 1854 she arrived at the British army hospital in Scutari (now Üsküdar, Istanbul) with 38 nurses. The hospital was overcrowded, dirty and short of supplies.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 2/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: She and the nurses improved cleanliness, food, blankets and beds. At night she walked the wards checking on patients, carrying a lamp.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 3/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: That is why she was called "the Lady with the Lamp". She also kept figures and showed that more patients died of disease than of their wounds.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 4/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: She presented the data as a circular diagram divided into wedges, so officials could grasp it quickly. She became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 5/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: In 1860 she opened a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London. Her story asks us to keep things clean and use data to help others.
clips.note: Florence Nightingale (1820–1910): panel 6/6 of "Nightingale and her lamp" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-m).

clips.text: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa, Italy, on 15 February 1564. He liked to test ideas with experiments and measurements.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 1/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: In his time many people believed every heavenly body circled the Earth. Galileo wanted to see the sky more clearly.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 2/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: In 1609 he built his own telescope and pointed it at the sky. He saw mountains and valleys on the Moon.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 3/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: From 7 January 1610 he watched Jupiter night after night, drawing the bright dots beside it. The dots moved: four moons were circling Jupiter.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 4/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: His findings supported the idea that the Earth goes around the Sun, an idea many people opposed. In 1633 he was tried in Rome and confined to his home for the rest of his life.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 5/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Even confined at home he kept writing; his book on motion came out in 1638. Galileo died on 8 January 1642, leaving an example: observe carefully, record, and test again.
clips.note: Galileo Galilei (1564–1642): panel 6/6 of "Galileo and the moons of Jupiter" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Maria Skłodowska was born in Warsaw, in today's Poland, on 7 November 1867. In 1891 she moved to Paris to study at the Sorbonne.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 1/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: In 1896 scientists found that uranium gives off invisible rays. Marie wanted to know where the rays came from, and whether other elements did the same.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 2/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: With her husband Pierre Curie she studied a uranium ore called pitchblende. In 1898 they announced two new elements: polonium and radium.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 3/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: To prove it, they processed tons of ore in a simple laboratory. In 1902 Marie obtained one-tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 4/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, then won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. She was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 5/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Marie Curie died on 4 July 1934, probably from years of exposure to radiation. Her story asks us to research patiently and with care for safety.
clips.note: Marie Skłodowska-Curie (1867–1934): panel 6/6 of "Marie Curie and radium" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Wilbur and Orville Wright were brothers from Dayton, Ohio, in the United States. In 1892 they opened a bicycle shop.
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 1/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Bicycle work sharpened their skills, and its profits paid for their flying experiments. The big problem: how do you control a machine in the air?
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 2/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Wilbur watched birds and got the idea of twisting the wingtips to keep balance. From 1900 they tested gliders at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 3/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Their 1901 glider did not lift as the figures predicted, so they built a wind tunnel and tested about 200 wing shapes. In 1902 they made hundreds of glides.
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 4/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: On 17 December 1903 Orville flew their powered aircraft for 12 seconds, about 37 metres (120 feet). On the fourth flight that day Wilbur flew for 59 seconds, about 260 metres (852 feet).
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 5/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: That short flight opened the age of the aeroplane. Their story asks us to learn from failure and test again with our own data.
clips.note: Wilbur Wright (1867–1912) dan Orville Wright (1871–1948): panel 6/6 of "The Wright brothers and the first flight" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: B.J. Habibie was born in Parepare, South Sulawesi, on 25 June 1936. He studied aeronautical engineering in Aachen, Germany, and earned his doctorate in 1965.
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 1/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: An aircraft's body can crack little by little through constant use. At the time engineers found it hard to calculate how small cracks spread.
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 2/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: While working in Germany's aircraft industry, Habibie helped develop ways to calculate how cracks spread. That earned him the nickname "Mr Crack".
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 3/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Once cracks could be calculated, aircraft could be designed lighter while staying safe.
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 4/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: In 1974 he returned to Indonesia to build an aircraft industry, now PT Dirgantara Indonesia. On 10 August 1995 the N-250 Gatotkaca, built by IPTN, made its first flight in Bandung.
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 5/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: That date is now marked as National Technology Awakening Day. Habibie died on 11 September 2019; his story asks us to master knowledge and use it for our country.
clips.note: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie (1936–2019): panel 6/6 of "Habibie and the N-250" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-h).

clips.text: Mohandas Gandhi was born in Porbandar, India, on 2 October 1869. He studied law in London and became a lawyer.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 1/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: In 1893 he went to work in South Africa. There he was forced off a first-class train carriage because of the colour of his skin.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 2/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Gandhi chose to resist injustice without violence. He called his method satyagraha, meaning holding firmly to truth.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 3/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Back in India, he urged people to spin thread and weave their own cloth. The spinning wheel became a symbol of self-reliance.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 4/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: On 12 March 1930 he began the Salt March, walking about 385 km to the coast at Dandi. There, on 6 April, he picked up a handful of salt in peaceful protest against the salt tax.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 5/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: India became independent in 1947, and Gandhi died on 30 January 1948. His birthday, 2 October, is now marked by the UN as the International Day of Non-Violence.
clips.note: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948): panel 6/6 of "Gandhi and the Salt March" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Nelson Mandela was born in Mvezo, South Africa, on 18 July 1918. He later became a lawyer in Johannesburg.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 1/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: South Africa then had apartheid, laws that separated people and treated them unequally by race. Mandela became one of the leaders of the movement against it.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 2/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: He was in prison from 1962 to 1990, 27 years in all. In prison he kept studying and kept hope alive.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 3/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: He was freed on 11 February 1990. He chose negotiation and reconciliation, not revenge.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 4/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: In 1993 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F.W. de Klerk for working to end apartheid peacefully. In 1994 he became South Africa's first president elected democratically by all its citizens.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 5/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Mandela died on 5 December 2013; his birthday, 18 July, is marked as Nelson Mandela International Day. His story asks us to choose dialogue and have the courage to forgive.
clips.note: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918–2013): panel 6/6 of "Mandela and the road to reconciliation" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Sejong became the fourth king of Korea's Joseon dynasty in 1418 and reigned until 1450. In 1420 he founded the Jiphyeonjeon, the "Hall of Worthies", for scholars.
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 1/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: At the time Koreans wrote with Chinese characters, which took years to master. Most ordinary people could not put their thoughts into writing.
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 2/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Sejong designed a simple new script. In 1443 he completed 28 letters: 17 consonants and 11 vowels.
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 3/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Some officials opposed the new script. Sejong carried on, and in 1446 it was proclaimed in the book Hunminjeongeum, "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People".
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 4/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Sejong's reign also produced a standard rain gauge. With it, rainfall across the kingdom could be recorded for farming.
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 5/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Today the script is called Hangul and used by millions; the Hunminjeongeum book is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. His story asks us to make knowledge easy for everyone to reach.
clips.note: Raja Sejong Agung / King Sejong the Great (1397–1450): panel 6/6 of "King Sejong and the Hangul alphabet" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Louis Braille was born in Coupvray, France, on 4 January 1809. His father made leather harness for horses.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 1/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: At the age of three he had an accident in his father's workshop. Soon afterwards he lost the sight of both eyes.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 2/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: In 1819, on a scholarship, he entered the school for blind children in Paris. Books for blind readers then used large raised letters that were heavy and slow to read.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 3/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Charles Barbier, a former army officer, showed the school a writing system of raised dots. Louis simplified it into a cell of six dots that fits under one fingertip.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 4/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: From 1826 he taught at the school, and in 1829, aged 20, he published his method. He also adapted the system for writing music.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 5/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Louis Braille died in 1852, and today braille is used all over the world; 4 January is World Braille Day. His story asks us to design things everyone can use.
clips.note: Louis Braille (1809–1852): panel 6/6 of "Louis Braille and the six dots" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Cut Nyak Dhien was born in 1848 in Lampadang, Aceh Besar, into a noble family. She grew up in a community devoted to faith and custom.
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 1/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: From 1873 Aceh was caught in a long war with the Dutch colonial government. Many families lost homes and loved ones, Cut Nyak Dhien among them.
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 2/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: After her husband Teuku Umar fell in 1899, she led her people herself. She kept her group together as they moved through the forests and mountains of Aceh.
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 3/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Years in the forest left her frail and ill, with failing eyes and painful joints. Pang Laot, her loyal follower, pitied her condition and in 1905 told the Dutch where she was.
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 4/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: She was exiled to Sumedang in West Java. There she taught religion to the local people, who called her "Ibu Perbu".
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 5/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).

clips.text: Cut Nyak Dhien died in Sumedang on 6 November 1908 and was named a National Hero in 1964. Her story asks us to stand by others and keep sharing knowledge, even in hard times.
clips.note: Cut Nyak Dhien (1848–1908): panel 6/6 of "Cut Nyak Dhien: leading and caring" (Sejarah adults, sej-a-x).
